title: Child World (1962–1992): the castle-front toy chain · Spectre Brands
description: Child World was the No. 2 U.S. toy chain, with castle-front stores. Weighed down by its parent’s debt, it stopped paying bills in 1990 and liquidated in 1992.

card.blurb: A Massachusetts toy supermarket with castle turrets and a roller-skating panda, and for years the No. 2 toy chain in America. Squeezed by Toys “R” Us and loaded with its parent’s debt, it stopped paying its bills in December 1990 and liquidated in 1992.

hero.dates: Founded in Quincy, Massachusetts, in 1962. Liquidated in 1992.
hero.standfirst: It built toy stores that looked like castles. Its owners built it a moat of debt.
hero.deck: Child World, founded in Quincy, Massachusetts, in 1962, grew into the country’s second-largest toy retailer and liquidated every store in 1992. It ran Children’s Palace stores alongside its own. Cole National bought it in 1981 and floated 18% of it in 1985; then Cole itself went through two leveraged buyouts. By 1990 the chain had about 180 stores, was losing money against [Toys “R” Us](/toys-r-us/), and was for sale. Roy Disney’s Trefoil walked away on Thanksgiving Day. Two weeks later Child World stopped paying $122M of bank debt and $212M owed for merchandise. Former Toys “R” Us executives took control in 1991, but in May 1992 it filed for Chapter 11, and by the autumn every store was closed. The account rests on contemporary reports in the Los Angeles Times, UPI and the New York Times, and on the bankruptcy court’s own findings.

findings.title: It was a copy of the leader.
findings.text: A trade editor said in 1990 that Child World had not set itself apart from Toys “R” Us “and they got their heads handed to them.”[^2] Toys “R” Us held about a quarter of the $13.5 billion American toy market.[^2]

findings.title: Its owner needed the money more than it did.
findings.text: Its parent, CNC Holding, the former Cole National, had been through two leveraged buyouts and was trying to sell Child World to cut its own debt. It could not pay to remodel or expand the chain.[^2][^3][^12]

findings.title: One lost buyer started the run.
findings.text: Trefoil backed out on Thanksgiving 1990 and the shares nearly halved. Two weeks later the chain stopped paying its banks and suppliers, and Mattel and Tyco were projected to take $46M of bad debts between them.[^3][^5] (derived)

findings.title: The rescue lasted a year.
findings.text: Former Toys “R” Us executives took control in 1991. In January 1992 the chain closed 26 stores in Chicago and Texas; in May it filed for bankruptcy; by autumn it was gone.[^1][^6][^7][^10]
